references.text: I [ref:1 Kings 9:7|1. Kongebok 9:7] warn God that the temple ("the house") will be abandoned and rejected if the people turn away. Jesus' words "See, your house is left to you" reflect this judgment over the temple.

[ref:Jer 12:7|Jeremiah 12:7]: "I have forsaken my house, I have cast off my inheritance." The Lord leaves his house – a parallel to Jesus' words that God's house will be left to them, empty and abandoned.

[ref:Jer 22:5|Jeremiah 22:5]: "But if you do not hear these words, I swear by myself," says the Lord, "that this house shall become a ruin." A prophetic warning that God's house will be destroyed, as Jesus' words reflect.

Jesus' quote "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" is taken directly from [ref:Ps 118:26|Psalm 118:26]. This messianic psalm was used at festive processions to the temple and is cited here as a condition for Israel to see Jesus again.

[ref:Matt 23:38-39|Matthew 23:38-39] is the parallel passage where Jesus speaks the same words about the house being left abandoned and that they will not see him until they say, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

At Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, the crowd cries out the words from [ref:Luke 19:38|Luke 19:38]: "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!" – a partial fulfillment of Jesus' prophecy in 13:35.

[ref:Luke 21:24|Luke 21:24] speaks of Jerusalem's destruction and that the city shall be "trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" – an elaboration on the judgment over the house that Jesus prophesies in 13:35.

[ref:Luke 13:34|Luke 13:34] is the immediate context where Jesus laments over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and whom he wanted to gather under his wings – the background for the judgment spoken in verse 35.

[ref:Hos 3:5|Hosea 3:5]: "Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God." Jesus' condition "until you say, Blessed is he who comes" points to a future repentance, which Hosea also prophesies about.

[ref:Rom 11:25-26|Romans 11:25-26] speaks of all Israel being saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in – a Pauline parallel to Jesus' promise that Jerusalem will one day welcome him with blessing.
